# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and pharmacology

Heart failure (HF) management has long centred on antagonising the maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic activation. Complementing this, the natriuretic peptide system promotes natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic and antihypertrophic effects, while suppressing RAAS and adrenergic outflow. Because neprilysin degrades natriuretic peptides (along with bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and other vasoactive peptides), its inhibition augments these protective signals [1]. Combining neprilysin inhibition with RAAS blockade is essential, since neprilysin inhibition alone is insufficient and combined neprilysin/ACE inhibition causes unacceptable angioedema. This was demonstrated in OVERTURE, where the vasopeptidase inhibitor omapatrilat was not more effective than enalapril in reducing the combined risk of death or hospitalization for heart failure requiring intravenous treatment among 5770 patients with NYHA class II–IV heart failure, and carried excess angioedema risk [2].

Sacubitril/valsartan (LCZ696) circumvents this by pairing the angiotensin II type-1 receptor blocker valsartan with the neprilysin-inhibitor prodrug sacubitril rather than an ACE inhibitor. LCZ696 is a single molecule comprising valsartan and the NEP-inhibitor prodrug AHU377 in a 1:1 ratio; oral administration causes dose-dependent increases in natriuretic peptide immunoreactivity, and treatment is associated with increases in plasma cGMP, renin concentration and activity, and angiotensin II, providing evidence for both neprilysin inhibition and angiotensin receptor blockade [3].

## HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF trial established ARNI as superior to ACE inhibition. Compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73–0.87), all-cause mortality (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.76–0.93), and HF hospitalisation (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.71–0.89) [4]. The trial was stopped prematurely after a median follow-up of 27 months on the recommendation of the data safety monitoring board owing to compelling evidence favouring sacubitril/valsartan [4]. Beyond hard endpoints, ARNI reduced the need for intensification of HF therapy and emergency department visits for worsening HF compared with enalapril [5].

Mechanistic studies clarified these benefits. In PROVE-HF, reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months, suggesting reverse cardiac remodelling [6]. By contrast, EVALUATE-HF found that sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril did not reduce central aortic stiffness, although some measures of diastolic function improved [7], implying that benefit derives from myocardial rather than vascular effects.

## In-hospital and acute settings

Two trials extended ARNI use to hospitalised patients. PIONEER-HF showed that among patients hospitalised for acute decompensated HF, initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to a greater reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril, with no significant difference in worsening renal function, hyperkalaemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [8]; an exploratory analysis showed lower rates of HF rehospitalisation [9]. TRANSITION confirmed feasibility, assessing tolerability and optimal timing of initiation in patients stabilised after acute HF, supporting either pre- or early post-discharge initiation [10]. After myocardial infarction, however, PARADISE-MI was neutral: sacubitril–valsartan was not associated with a significantly lower incidence of death from cardiovascular causes or incident heart failure than ramipril among patients with acute myocardial infarction [11], although exploratory recurrent-event analyses favoured ARNI [12].

## Preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction

The phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial showed that in HFpEF, LCZ696 reduced NT-proBNP to a greater extent than valsartan at 12 weeks and was well tolerated, although whether these effects would translate into improved outcomes needed prospective testing [13]. The definitive PARAGON-HF trial was, however, narrowly negative: sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total HF hospitalisations and cardiovascular death among patients with an ejection fraction of 45% or higher [14] (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.75–1.01) [15]. Subgroup signals suggested benefit in women and those with below-median ejection fraction [16]. A pooled analysis across the EF spectrum reinforced this gradient of benefit [17], and the PARALLAX trial found that sacubitril/valsartan improved NT-proBNP but failed to improve submaximal exercise capacity [18]. PARAGLIDE-HF, in patients with EF >40% and recent worsening HF, again showed greater natriuretic-peptide reduction with ARNI [19]; a prespecified pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analysis found that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced total worsening HF events and cardiovascular death in patients with recent worsening HF [20].

## Guidelines and clinical positioning

Reflecting this evidence, contemporary guidelines endorse ARNI. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline addresses the full EF spectrum, classifying HFrEF as LVEF ≤40%, HFmrEF as 41–49%, and HFpEF as ≥50% [21], and recommends ARNI as a foundational therapy for HFrEF alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors. The 2021 ESC guidelines similarly recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a class I therapy in HFrEF [22], with the 2023 focused update incorporating subsequent trial data [23]. Pooled and remodelling analyses continue to support replacing ACE inhibitors/ARBs with ARNI even in apparently stable patients [24,25], and ARNI initiation soon after decompensation is now standard [26].

## Safety, limitations, and future directions

ARNI is generally well tolerated. The principal adverse effects are symptomatic hypotension and, less commonly, angioedema; rates of renal dysfunction and hyperkalaemia are comparable to ACE inhibition [4,8]. A mandatory 36-hour washout from ACE inhibitors mitigates angioedema risk, and the pharmacology of sacubitril—whose active metabolite does not inhibit aminopeptidase P—confers a lower angioedema risk than omapatrilat [27]. Trial findings have informed device and quality-of-life endpoints [28] and prognostic biomarker interpretation [29], while long-term data continue to refine optimal dosing and patient selection [30].

In summary, sacubitril/valsartan is a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy with robust mortality and morbidity benefits, has an established role across the in-hospital continuum, and offers more modest, EF-dependent benefit in HFpEF/HFmrEF. Ongoing work focuses on earlier initiation, broader phenotyping, and integration within quadruple guideline-directed therapy.
